articles.title: Scientists discover a bacterial defense so strange they thought it was broken
articles.description: Scientists have discovered a bizarre bacterial defense system that works almost completely backward from anything seen before. Unlike typical bacterial immune systems that keep a deadly toxin under control until a virus attacks, this unusual mechanism waits until an infection begins before producing the DNA that switches on its lethal weapon. The infected bacterium then destroys itself, preventing the virus from multiplying and spreading to neighboring cells.

articles.title: Bodian Seminar: Translating sensations to perceptions across species
articles.description: How do you know to stretch out your left hand to catch a ball thrown at you from the left? How do you know where to look when you hear a sound coming from behind you? Somewhere between the light entering your eyes or the sound entering your ears, your brain has to turn that collection of sensory signals into something meaningful. In a Bodian Seminar hosted by the Zanvyl Krieger Mind/Brain Institute on Oct. 19, guest speaker Madineh Sedigh-Sarvestani focused on answering these exact questions. Sedigh-Sarvestani is an Assistant Professor of Neurobiology & Behaviour at Cornell University, and her lab focuses on understanding how our brains and bodies translate sensation into perception. At the center of her research is the idea of a "sensory-motor dictionary." "Our core hypothesis is that sensation doesn't come pre-labeled with meaning," Sedigh-Sarvestani explained. The idea is that movements of the body produce predictable changes in sensory information. Over time, the brain learns these relationships and uses them to understand the world. "The dictionary is rooted in body movements," she said. One example of the distinction between sensation and perception comes from adults who undergo cataract-removal surgery after many years of limited vision. Following a successful surgery, patients can immediately detect light and other visual information, but they may need weeks to recognize familiar people and objects. The theory of the sensory-motor dictionary led Sedigh-Sarvestani to an unusual species: treeshrews. Treeshrews have eyes positioned on the side of their heads, similar to mice and rats. Based on this eye placement, researchers expect to see tree shrews relying on head movements rather than eye movements to shift their gaze. Primates, by comparison, can move their eyes independently of their heads to change what they're looking at. Sedigh-Sarvestani's research demonstrates that treeshrews may occupy an unusual position between these two groups. Studying just the pupils of head-fixed treeshrews; she observed that they were able to make small, five-degree eye movements, 90% of which were without any head movement at all. "Much of their visual system seems specialized for sampling the binocular field in front of them," Sedigh-Sarvestani said. But why? A treeshrew doesn't need to look at an iPhone or interpret facial expressions. Their highly specialized vision frontal is surprising for a small, nonsocial animal. Sedigh-Sarvestani hypothesized that the animal's unique ability to control their visual system comes from their body movements. During the seminar, Sedigh-Sarvestani showed footage of a treeshrew in her lab leaping between branches in its enclosure, and executing an almost 180 degree rotation in the air to easily land on the next branch. A treeshrew jumping between branches may need to move its head and body in one direction while keeping its eyes oriented toward a landing point. Independent eye movements could allow the animal to maintain useful visual information even while its body is rotating through space. To test whether motor information actually contributes to perception, the lab changed the relationship between movement and visual input. In one experiment, tree shrews were trained to move their gaze toward a visual target. Researchers then reversed the relationship between eye movement and the target's movement, so that moving their eyes in one direction caused the target to move in the opposite direction. The animals were able to adapt to the new relationship within a matter of weeks. Sedigh-Sarvestani is pursuing this question further through experiments involving treeshrew-sized goggles with inverting prisms. The specially designed goggles make the animals' visual world appear upside down, forcing them to adapt to a fundamentally different relationship between their movements and what they see. This is an experiment that can easily be done on humans - many students may even encounter a version in their introductory psychology classes - but it can be very difficult to execute on animals. As Sedigh-Sarvestani put it, "[Tree shrews] are highly mobile, and their movements require vision." Thus, they are good candidates for this style of experiment. The animals initially struggled to navigate the altered environment. They hesitated to execute their previous amazing acrobatic jumps. Over time, however, they began to adjust their movements and eventually regained the ability to perform complex behaviors such as jumping between branches. If visual neurons change their responses as an animal learns a new relationship between movement and vision, such as completely flipping the visual field upside down, it would suggest that perception is not based solely on what reaches the retina. Instead, the brain may incorporate information about the body's movements to determine what those sensory signals mean. For Sedigh-Sarvestani, understanding this relationship could provide a new way of thinking about perception itself. Rather than passively receiving information from the world, the brain may constantly learn what its sensations mean through the body's interactions with its environment. The ability to catch a ball, navigate a branch or simply recognize an object may therefore depend on a sensory-motor dictionary that the brain has spent a lifetime learning to read.

articles.title: Wherever you go, there you are!
articles.description: It's been a little over a month since I started college, but I continue to find myself trapped in the cycle of meeting new people and then confronting the inevitable small talk. I am aware I should be grateful to still be meeting new, kind, and interesting people - and I am! - but I thoroughly dread the perplexing question that invariably follows: Where are you from? I've reached a monotonous state in which I simply answer Seattle. I actually live in the suburbs (sue me), but if I say Washington, chances are the freshman will eagerly ask, "D.C.?" and then I am forced to quash the exciting prospect of me being a local tour guide with the anticlimactic clarification of Washington State. This is admittedly not a big deal. But I, too, am an exhausted freshman at Hopkins and, in the interest of optimizing my time and preserving my sanity, do not wish to divulge my entire life story to this person in my 200-person lecture hall whom I may or may not ever see again. At least take me out to dinner first! But it is important to be sociable, and I actually am a caring person, so the conversation usually continues. They ask me a follow up question about Grey's Anatomy and Seattle, and suddenly my story begins to unravel. "Well, actually, I've only lived in Seattle for two years" "Oh, so where are you really from?" No! Now I am trapped sharing my life story. Well, before that, I lived in Florida for a while. But I hated Florida. I feel compelled to make this distinction known. Perhaps I am being pretentious, unwilling to be associated with "Florida man" and all that transpires down there, but I cannot help myself. I usually explain I hated the heat, which is entirely true. The only thing I loathe more than this conversation is the humidity in Baltimore. "But are you from there?" No. Well, actually, I was born in Beijing and lived there for six years until my parents decided to move back to the U.S., eventually settling in Florida. It was cheaper, okay? Now I am presumably asked why my parents moved there, to which I have no answer. And don't get me wrong: I absolutely loved Beijing. It was my first home, and I cherish the culture and everything it imparted on me. But it feels slightly presumptuous for me, a white girl, to claim that I understand that experience when, in this particular moment, I only receive the favorable end of it. That is - an interesting conversation starter. Now I am stuck feeling as though this conversation, in which we are supposedly getting to know each other, has become entirely centered upon me and my life, when you were probably just being polite. You did not ask for the synopsis of my existence. And maybe, selfishly, I am writing this very article in the hopes that people read it and not have to ask me this question. This brings me to my final qualm: what does "where are you from?" even mean? I am privileged in that I do not have to deal with people looking condescendingly as they ask someone where they are "originally" from. But I would like to think I am not alone in this confusion. The question itself seems woefully underspecified. What if we collectively agreed to ask, "Where did you last live?" But, to play devil's advocate - and put my philosophical hat on - am I the problem with today's society? We are all so focused on achieving our next goal and optimizing every spare moment that a simple question, one that could potentially lead to more conversation, becomes dreadful. And is that not the very essence of communication? That those small, even awkward moments, can lead to lasting connections? That an unassuming question can reveal something far more substantial? Or perhaps I am putting too much pressure on this interaction in its entirety. Maybe no one cares what I am answering, nor are they listening with the attention that I am imagining. Maybe they, too, are simply hoping to move on with their day. Ultimately, though, I can fall into existentialism. What even is the act of "from" somewhere? What does telling you where I am from actually reveal about me? Oftentimes, our living situations are merely circumstantial. Maybe the fact that I have moved fairly frequently tells you I am trying to escape myself. Or maybe my parents were in the military. They were not. I suppose this is the point of small talk. The question itself is not necessarily meant to produce a meaningful answer; it is intended to open the door to a new bond. Perhaps the places we come from do matter. Of course, our environments shape our formative years and influence the people we ultimately become. But if we are talking about the one-word answer of a city or county, does that really tell me much about you? I propose an amendment. I think this question is inherently flawed. What if we asked, "Where are you going?" Then you can tell me about where you are from if it serves a relevant purpose or if you so please. But I personally would much rather hear about your aspirations or what excites you, as that makes you, you. As they say: "Wherever you go, there you are!" Mirabelle DeAngelis is a freshman from Bellevue, Wash. majoring in Applied Mathematics and Statistics.

articles.title: The next great founder may be hiding in healthcare
articles.description: Academic medical centers and universities produce groundbreaking research every day. An autism researcher who builds an AI game to clinically improve behavioral problems. A basic scientist who discovers how the environment of tumors impacts treatment. An electrical engineer who nano-sized a method for magnets to image the body. An MBA who teamed up with two MDs to create a novel approach to solving complex pediatric cardiac cases. And all are at risk of remaining stuck in the ivory tower. Venture capital is great at finding founders who tell a compelling story with confidence, but the best founders may not innately exhibit those traits. This is particularly true in healthcare, where physicians, researchers, PhDs, and faculty members often have the deep technical understanding and firsthand experience needed to build the next great company. These scientists and clinicians are knee-deep in the problems they’re trying to solve. They’ve seen where existing approaches fall short, often for years, and have developed ideas for how to do things differently. But getting those ideas into the market requires a different set of skills. They need to learn how to test the market hypothesis, not just the scientific hypothesis. Today, there are researchers and scientists developing promising healthcare innovations who aren’t thinking about building a company. And if they are, many show up to pitch venture capitalists with presentations better suited for an academic keynote or scientific meeting. Slides dense in technical detail, with little market analysis or validation, and without much of a story. It’s not surprising that many VCs pass. But how many promising ideas are we missing because the people behind them haven’t learned how to pitch? Our experience We’ve seen this firsthand, over and over again. And it’s made us rethink what it actually means to invest early. Funds have competed for years to get into the best deals as early as possible. But in healthcare, getting in early may mean investing before there’s even a company. Before there’s a pitch deck, a business model, or a founder who has fully embraced the idea of becoming an entrepreneur. This is the idea behind inception investing. Rather than starting with a company and evaluating whether it’s worth backing, the starting point is a person who is particularly well suited to solving a problem. That might be a clinician or researcher with decades of experience and a scientific approach that hasn’t yet been commercialized. Or it might be someone whose personal experience with the healthcare system has led them to become deeply focused on a problem that others have overlooked. In either case, there may be no company yet. The market might not be defined. The founder might not know how to tell a compelling story. But those aren’t necessarily reasons to walk away. At Treehub, we’ve found that the qualities we’re looking for in these early conversations are often different from what a traditional investor might prioritize. We’re less concerned with whether someone can deliver a polished pitch and more interested in whether they understand a problem well enough to build something that hasn’t existed before. More than just science Of course, scientific expertise alone doesn’t make a successful founder. There still needs to be a market for the solution, a viable business model, and a path to getting it into patients’ hands. And not every researcher wants to build a company. But those are questions worth exploring with someone who has spent years developing a potentially important solution, rather than reasons to dismiss them at the outset. A scientist can learn how to evaluate a market. A physician can find a commercial partner. A researcher can learn how to tell a story that resonates with investors. The experience that led them to the idea in the first place is much harder to replicate. If we want more of the research coming out of universities and academic medical centers to reach patients, we need to get better at identifying the people behind it and helping them figure out what comes next. The next great healthcare company may not exist yet. And the person who will build it may still be thinking of themselves as a scientist, physician, or researcher rather than a founder. That’s exactly why we should be looking for them now.
